title: Agent Mosaic Leaks, Unified Routing, and Serverless Multi-Turn RL
intro: Today's updates highlight a subtle authorization flaw when agents aggregate retrieved documents, along with a unified routing method that jointly optimizes execution modes. We also look at a serverless harness for multi-turn agent RL and a few practical serving updates.

stories.headline: Mosaic leaks: When safe retrievals combine into unsafe disclosures
stories.summary: A new paper, *Agent Mosaic*, highlights a security failure mode in agentic RAG: an agent retrieves multiple individually permitted documents and synthesizes an unauthorized sensitive composite conclusion. Testing across 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military scenarios produced non-negligible leak rates; even the best model evaluated, GPT-5.6-Sol, leaked forbidden composites in 7.08% of simulated responses under benign queries, with higher rates observed in live agent harnesses. While visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules helped, unsafe disclosures persisted in 32.37% of simulated answers across all intents. Notably, simply ramping up refusals does not solve the issue, as significant refusals often inadvertently confirmed the prohibited conclusions.
stories.why_it_matters: Document-level ACLs fall short when the security risk is the context-window join; if you build RAG agents for mixed-clearance users, system prompts won't catch synthesis leaks.
stories.reason: Exposes a critical agentic vulnerability where autonomous agents synthesize unclassified documents into unauthorized disclosures of sensitive, confidential information.

item.content:
Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
Abstract
LLM agents frequently leak sensitive conclusions assembled from multiple confidential documents, and common safeguards fail to eliminate this mosaic-style disclosure risk.
Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. We quantify its realization with 30 synthetic cybersecurity, medical, and military examples, yielding 10,800 final answers from three LLM agents in controlled simulation and 1,440 answers from live agents in two open-source harnesses. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.
Community
We introduce Agent Mosaic, a study of confidentiality leaks in LLM agents where combining individually accessible information reveals sensitive conclusions. Through evaluations across simulated and live agents, we show that such leaks occur even under benign queries and persist despite explicit safeguards. Benchmark dataset and code TBP.

Every agent deployment I've audited has the same hole: per-document ACLs that look fine one retrieval at a time. Nothing in the trace is individually wrong — the leak is the join, three documents that were each permitted sitting in one context window and producing an answer none of them contained alone. So the part I care about isn't the 30 hand-built examples, it's whether this holds up on a corpus where you can't enumerate the combinations. What I'd actually deploy is duller than a classifier: log the retrieval set per answer, then flag any claim that only holds if you combine documents the requesting user couldn't have opened side by side. That's a provenance check, and it scales past a curated test set. The fix at assembly time is duller still — scope retrieval to the intersection of what the user is cleared for before the context exists, rather than a system prompt asking the agent to be careful.

stories.headline: RouteWeaver: Jointly optimizing execution mode and model selection
stories.summary: Existing routing pipelines typically lock into a fixed paradigm, choosing models purely within single-round, multi-round, or agentic frameworks. *RouteWeaver* introduces a unified policy that dynamically decides both *how* to execute (the routing mode) and *which* heterogeneous model to invoke at each step. To train this without mode collapse, the authors developed COMET-GRPO, which separates trajectory-level advantages into distinct credit signals for mode selection versus execution, coupled with progressive exploration to bootstrap execution competency first. Across benchmarks spanning math, code, logic, and factual recall, the framework hit 61.4% average accuracy, an 11.03% relative improvement over the best baseline.
stories.why_it_matters: Dynamically picking whether a query needs a single cheap call or an iterative agentic loop avoids the cost of hardcoding one execution paradigm across varied tasks.
stories.reason: Introduces a unified routing architecture that dynamically alternates between single-turn, multi-turn, and autonomous agentic execution paradigms based on task complexity.

item.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
item.summary: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. item.content:
RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
Abstract
RouteWeaver unifies heterogeneous LLM routing modes via coordinated training and progressive exploration, improving accuracy across diverse reasoning tasks.
LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode–Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

stories.headline: OpenAI details offline isolation for frontier training
stories.summary: OpenAI shared details on how it has tightened containment for frontier model training and evaluation environments. The updated setup cuts off direct internet access during training runs and pairs that offline isolation with high-compute red-teaming infrastructure. While technical implementation details in the public note remain sparse, the isolation boundary targets autonomous exfiltration and training-time harness exploitation as capability thresholds advance.
stories.why_it_matters: Shows the hardening pattern frontier labs are using to contain agentic capabilities and red-team runs before deployment.
stories.reason: Details the offline sandboxing, containment, and compute-heavy red-teaming infrastructure OpenAI built to isolate frontier models and agents during training.

stories.headline: Ollama v0.40.11 adds streaming speech and d3 decision models
stories.summary: Ollama's v0.40.11 release brings two notable capabilities to local runtimes: native macOS speech generation via Phonon and support for the `d3` decision model family. Audio can now stream out through an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint alongside real-time playback in the CLI. The release also integrates vLLM Semantic Router's `d3` models—ranging from 2B to 27B parameters—enabling fast local scoring, binary classification, and state evaluation for agent branching without invoking general-purpose chat models.
stories.why_it_matters: Local `d3` support gives agent harnesses low-overhead, dedicated classification primitives for routing and tool gating without hitting frontier APIs.
stories.reason: Ollama's new release adds an OpenAI-compatible speech streaming endpoint and integrates decision-model support directly into local serving runtimes.

stories.headline: OmniDR-Bench: Grading deep research agents on source videos
stories.summary: Most research agent benchmarks evaluate open-web synthesis, but *OmniDR-Bench* targets video-centered deep research where an agent must ground interactive, cited reports in specific video moments while retrieving supporting web evidence. The benchmark comprises 50 bilingual tasks spanning 19 domains evaluated against 6,414 atomic binary criteria using "Omni Atomic Rubric Trees" across audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence, and presentation. Testing 18 agent configurations showed considerable headroom: the top-performing system achieved a score of only 63.3 out of 100, struggling particularly with cross-modal causal reasoning and precise timestamped citations.
stories.why_it_matters: Gives agent builders a rigorous, rubric-calibrated eval for long-horizon multimodal research that goes well beyond standard text search.
stories.reason: Provides a comprehensive evaluation benchmark specifically measuring how deep research agents plan, investigate, and synthesize multimodal video sources.

item.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
item.summary: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent…
item.content:
Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
Abstract
Researchers introduce a benchmark and evaluation framework for video-centered deep research agents that synthesize external evidence into interactive reports linked to video moments.
Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.

stories.headline: AWS details multi-turn agent RL on SageMaker and AgentCore
stories.summary: AWS published a practical walkthrough of its Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) service, which trains agent policies on final trajectory completion rather than step-level imitation. Running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with GRPO, the training job invokes the agent environment once per rollout, allows multi-turn tool interaction (demonstrated on Wordle), and scores the policy purely on outcome rewards. Fine-tuning a LoRA adapter on `gpt-oss-20b` increased the solve rate from 15% to 69% under low reasoning effort for $339 in token spend across roughly 105,000 rollouts. Pricing decouples prefill, generation, and backward passes, with backward-pass tokens dominating costs due to re-reading accumulated conversation turns.
stories.why_it_matters: Provides a clean template for using outcome-driven GRPO to teach small, cheap models how to execute company-specific multi-step agent trajectories.
stories.reason: Provides a practical guide for training autonomous agents with multi-turn reinforcement learning evaluated against full trajectory task completion rather than step-level imitation.

item.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
item.summary: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on the outcome of a whole multi-step task rather than labeled steps. This hands-on guide walks the full pipeline using Wordle: deploying the agent and reward on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, and evaluating at serving settings.
item.content:
Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome.

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder . The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result.

This post uses Wordle , a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting.

In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models . All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository .

Solution overview

The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect.

Figure 1: MTRL on SageMaker AI, where the training job invokes the AgentCore-hosted agent once per rollout to sample the policy model, play the game, and report a reward

For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word , and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ) adapter on the policy model.

Three design points matter for what follows:

The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.

The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring.

The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier.

Supported models and AWS Regions

MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter:

Base model
AWS Regions

Amazon Nova 2 Lite

GPT-OSS-20B

Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned)
US West (Oregon) (us-west-2)

We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list.

Pricing

You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model:

Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history.

Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens.

Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter.

The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339:

The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage . See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates.

Prerequisites

To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites .

Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI ( npm install -g @aws/agentcore ). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs.

botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation.

Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1.

An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN.

Step 1: Create the IAM roles

MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention.

Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically.

Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession , and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy.

{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [{
"Effect": "Allow",
"Principal": {"Service": "job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com"},
"Action": ["sts:AssumeRole", "sts:TagSession"]
}]
}

Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com , not sagemaker.amazonaws.com . With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries.

related.title: Announcing new ways to customize models with SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs
related.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization now includes training sessions, generally available today. You write and coordinate your own post-training loop (custom loss functions, reward signals, or multi-turn reinforcement learning) while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.
related.content:
Companies getting real results from AI aren’t only using foundation models (FMs) off the shelf. They’re customizing open-weight models using post-training techniques such as reinforcement learning. A model trained on your business context, product catalog, or clinical vocabulary will be more accurate for your task and cost less to run. When you build agents, your data, workflows, evaluations, and success criteria also shape how the model behaves.

However, model customization is difficult. You must choose the right technique, set up and manage GPU infrastructure, and, for agents, build environments for multi-turn reinforcement learning. We launched Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to solve these challenges, and today, we’re expanding it with the general availability launch of training sessions.

With training sessions you get control over the post-training logic without managing the underlying infrastructure. You write and coordinate the training loop, including custom loss functions or reward signals. SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.

Customize without the hassles of infrastructure management

With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, you don’t choose instance types, manage clusters, or write distributed training configuration.

We didn’t want to limit you . You can use techniques such as SFT, DPO, RLVR, RLAIF, or multi-turn RL. You can choose how much of the model to update with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning and chain techniques together through continuous customization.

We didn’t want you to waste time . Our SageMaker AI training sessions cookbook provides examples and use cases, along with model customization agent skills. You describe your use case, and the agent handles data prep, technique choice, training, evaluation, and deployment. The agent works where you work, in SageMaker Studio, Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or GitHub Copilot.

“We adopted SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions to build a healthcare claim-denial triage model, and the experience validated the platform from day one. The low-level API surface, direct control over the forward and backward passes, sampling, and the optimizer step gave our scientists the fine-grained control they need to pursue reinforcement learning on a demanding, accuracy-critical use case. Training Sessions gives us the right primitives to push toward production-grade performance.”

— Rob Gontarek, Senior Vice President, Data Science, ImagineSoftware

Write your own post-training loop

One important shift in agent training is toward multi-turn reinforcement learning. For example, an agent that books travel, triages support tickets, or runs a multi-step research task needs several rounds of interaction before you can judge whether it reached the right outcome.

However, the training loop can get complicated quickly. You may train the model on one set of infrastructure, run inference on another to generate responses, score those responses, and feed the results into the next update. Each stage needs different compute, and connecting them across separate tools and clusters adds work.

SageMaker AI already offers multi-turn RL as a managed, serverless technique. But we heard from customers who wanted to define their own loss functions, shape reward signals, or RL stages in one loop. Training sessions give you that flexibility.

“With SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions, we fine-tuned gpt-oss-20b for agentic, multi-turn tool calling against our Amazon Neptune knowledge graph — and the platform handled the infrastructure for us. Setup just worked, with no manual tuning and no out-of-memory wrangling. Checkpoint-and-resume was a standout: resuming from an exact step was completely reliable. It gave our developers the flexibility they wanted while taking the operational burden off their plate.”

— Nitin Wagh, CEO, Karini AI

How it works

Your code runs the training loop and reward function in your environment and connects the agent to its tools or simulators. The training session performs the GPU-heavy work: a sampler generates responses, and a trainer calculates gradients and updates the model weights. The exact sequence depends on the algorithm you write.

For example, let’s look at Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) implementation. GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that generates several responses to the same prompt, scores them, and uses their relative performance to update the model. One pass through the loop works like this:

Sample responses –  Your loop asks the sampler to generate several responses for each prompt using the current model.

Score them –  Your reward function scores each response in your environment using a verifier, reward model, or test harness.

Update the model –  Your loop sends the scores back to the trainer. forward_backward() uses them to calculate gradients, and optim_step() applies the update to the model weights.

Refresh and repeat –  Your loop asks the session to refresh the sampler with the updated weights, then starts the next batch. Your code repeats these steps until training is complete.

You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes. The meter stops while your reward function scores a batch in your environment, and there is no capacity to reserve.

Keep control of your data and models

Each session uses an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you create, and you can add your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and virtual private cloud (VPC) configuration. Your data stays in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets in the AWS Region that you choose, and your checkpoints land there too.

We don’t use your data or your customized weights to train another model. Before deployment, you can evaluate the model for accuracy, bias, and safety. After you deploy, you can apply guardrails and monitor it with Amazon CloudWatch.

You can keep using the governance processes your teams already have.

Get started today

Write your own training loop on SageMaker AI serverless model customization training sessions, available today with support for gpt-oss-20b , gemma-4-31B-it , Qwen3.6-27B , and Qwen3.8-27B .

Two ways to get started:

In your IDE: Install the SageMaker Python SDK (on Linux or macOS with Python 3.10 to 3.12), clone the cookbook, and start developing.

In SageMaker Studio: Launch a ready-to-use AI development environment in under 20 seconds. Sign in, open a notebook, connect your coding agent (Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or Copilot), download the agent skills and cookbook, and you’re ready to begin.

related.title: Write your own training loop — without managing GPUs — with Amazon SageMaker training session APIs
related.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI training session APIs let you write your own LLM training loop (SFT, RL, or custom objectives) in a Python script while the service runs the GPUs. This post introduces the programming model and three SDK clients, then walks through a GRPO loop on GSM8K and a reinforcement learning workload on competitive programming.
related.content:
Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) today usually forces a tradeoff between training loop control and operational simplicity. With fully managed services you select a base model, provide data and hyperparameters, and the service owns everything else, which works well when a standard, prepackaged recipe fits your problem. Less managed services give you more control, but you also manage more of the underlying infrastructure and training frameworks. Sometimes a standard recipe isn’t enough: you need a custom loss or data curriculum for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), your own preference optimization, a reinforcement learning (RL) reward function, or an alignment algorithm published last week. As soon as you need to shape the training procedure yourself, you take on that infrastructure work to gain algorithmic freedom.

Today, serverless model customization in Amazon SageMaker AI expands with training session APIs, which remove that tradeoff by drawing the abstraction boundary one level lower. Instead of abstracting away the algorithm, they abstract away the compute. Operations like forward_backward() , optim_step() , and sample() become SageMaker API calls that you compose into whatever procedure your technique requires: SFT, preference optimization, RL, or something new. The calls target a live, stateful session, so the model stays loaded on the GPUs across steps, and you drive as many calls as you need against it. The service handles runtime setup, distributed execution, gradient synchronization, fault recovery, tenant isolation, and the operations of running GPUs at scale. You write the training loop, and SageMaker AI runs the infrastructure.

Alongside the service, we’re releasing the SageMaker training sessions cookbook , a set of ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes that you can use as blueprints for your own training loops.

In this post, we introduce the programming model and the three SDK clients, and show where training session APIs fit among the model training and customization options in SageMaker AI. We then take apart a minimal RL loop on grade-school math problems (GSM8K) to show how the operations fit together and finish with a real-world workload from the cookbook: reinforcement learning on competitive programming problems, where generated code is graded by running it against unit tests.

What are SageMaker AI training session APIs?

With SageMaker AI training session APIs, you can drive a live, GPU-backed session from your own Python process on your local machine. You call the operations, and SageMaker AI runs them on managed accelerators loaded with your chosen base model plus your Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter. There’s no config file describing the whole job up front and no cluster creation step. You control what happens at each step, interactively, from code, so you can iterate and debug quickly.

The division of responsibilities looks like this:

You focus on
You write
SageMaker AI handles

Your data, RL environments, agents, and algorithm
A Python training loop that calls operations such as forward_backward() , optim_step() , and sample() for the steps that need GPUs
GPU allocation, model and LoRA loading, distributed execution, fault recovery, checkpoint storage, security

The API is organized around three clients in the SageMaker Python SDK , created in sequence. A ServiceClient holds the platform-level settings (execution role, model package group, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) output location, and optionally an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and virtual private cloud (VPC) configuration, which you can also override per session) and starts a session. The ServiceClient instantiates a TrainingClient (training and checkpointing operations such as forward , forward_backward , optim_step , and save_weights_for_sampler ), which in turn instantiates a SamplingClient ( sample and compute_logprobs , for generation and scoring during rollouts and evaluation). Each API call maps to one operation in your loop. An active session also serves an OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint, so existing OpenAI client code can sample from it.

Figure 1: The SageMaker Python SDK client hierarchy for training session APIs

For reinforcement learning , the loop has a characteristic shape. The following figure shows one training step and where each part runs: the steps in green call APIs on service-managed GPUs, and the steps in purple, your loop control and reward logic, run on your machine.

Figure 2: One training step, with sampling, gradient, and checkpoint operations on managed GPUs and loop control and reward logic on your machine

Each step loads a batch of prompts and (1) samples from the current model on the GPU. Your Python code then (2) scores those outputs: a verifier, a reward-model call, a test harness, anything you can express in code. (3) forward_backward and optim_step turn the scores into a gradient update on the GPU, and (4) save_weights_and_get_sampling_client() refreshes the sampler so the next step draws from the updated model.

You own the data, the loop control, and the reward; SageMaker AI runs the GPU-bound sampling, gradient, and checkpoint operations. The same primitives cover supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and other LLM training techniques . For SFT, drop the sampling and reward steps and call forward_backward with a cross_entropy loss over labeled examples.

Who is this for and where does it fit within Amazon SageMaker AI?

Training session APIs are the right starting point when you need fast iteration cycles and algorithmic freedom, such as a custom loss, a new RL reward signal, or a multi-stage pipeline, but don’t want to provision or operate GPU infrastructure yourself.

Usage is billed per token processed, so you’re charged only for the compute your loop consumes. If your reward function takes 10 seconds to score a batch on your machine, no GPU time is billed while it runs. Compared with hourly GPU billing, this has two practical advantages. First, there’s no idle-GPU cost: reward computation, data loading, logging, and debugging happen off the clock, and you’re billed only when you call a GPU-bound operation. Second, cost scales with your dataset and generation volume, not with wall-clock time or cluster size, which makes spend easier to forecast and experiments easier to compare. The savings over reserving GPUs for the full session can be significant for workloads with heavy local computation, such as complex reward models, multi-tool agentic rollouts, or human-in-the-loop evaluation.

Training session APIs are built for teams whose work is defined by the training algorithm, not only the dataset. Because you compose the loop yourself, the same primitives support supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with a cross_entropy loss over labeled data, reinforcement learning with ppo , importance_sampling , or cispo (GRPO, PPO, and other group-relative methods), and custom objectives , such as preference optimization or distillation, built from the same pieces. They fit:

Post-training and alignment researchers implementing RL methods (GRPO, PPO, importance-sampling variants), custom advantage estimators, or new objectives.

Teams doing supervised fine-tuning or preference optimization who need a non-standard loss, a data curriculum, or a multi-stage pipeline that config-driven recipes don’t express.

Agentic and multi-turn RL builders who need custom rollout logic, reward shaping, and curricula.

Machine learning (ML) engineers who’ve outgrown config-driven fine-tuning but don’t want to own the operational burden of GPU clusters.

Researchers porting existing training-loop code, since the operation-based programming model maps directly onto loops written against low-level forward_backward , optim_step , and sample APIs.

The supported base models and the AWS Regions where each is available are listed in the training session APIs documentation .

Where training session APIs fit within Amazon SageMaker…

stories.headline: Meta Expert: Cross-layer sharing trims MoE redundancy
stories.summary: Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts architectures typically isolate experts within discrete layers, introducing redundant representations across the network depth. A new paper proposes *Meta Expert*, sharing expert parameters across layers rather than restricting them to local layer boundaries. In empirical tests, Meta Expert matches vanilla MoE loss and downstream performance while using only 70% to 80% of the expert count and 75% to 90% of total parameters, with savings scaling up on deeper models. The architecture, which also provides flexible residual pathways for token routing, has been rolled out in the open-weight Intern-S2-Mobius release.
stories.why_it_matters: Cross-layer parameter sharing cuts overall parameter footprint and cache pressure, easing the memory-bandwidth bottlenecks that hit MoE serving.
stories.reason: Proposes cross-layer expert sharing in Mixture-of-Experts architectures to significantly reduce storage and memory bandwidth overhead during MoE serving.

item.content:
Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE
Abstract
Shared meta-experts across layers reduce redundancy and improve efficiency compared to layer-specific local experts in mixture-of-experts models.
As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.
Community
A comparison between the Vanilla and Meta-Expert models shows that, when trained under the optimal settings of the Vanilla model at varying depths and scales, models with Meta Experts achieve loss comparable to the Vanilla baselines while using only 70–80% as many experts, or 75–90% as many parameters. Notably, the savings in both experts and parameters grow as the models become deeper and larger, demonstrating the favorable scalability of Meta Experts.
The proposed method has been scaled up in Intern-S2-Mobius, which is available at https://github.com/InternLM/Intern-S2-Mobius and https://huggingface.co/internlm/Intern-S2-Mobius.
Interesting research! It’s always good to see people exploring new ideas and pushing technology forward. quick_hits.line: Microsoft Research introduced Flint-interactive, a specialized language that lets agents generate interactive, filterable data visualizations.

item.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
item.summary:
Flint-interactive gives AI agents a language for creating interactive visualizations. Click a chart, filter data, highlight related content, and explore beyond the view the author originally chose.

The post Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations appeared first on Microsoft Research .
item.content:
At a glance

Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.

Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.

Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.

Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another.

AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering:

(As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select?

(As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data?

Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face:

High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time.

Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them.

These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions.

PODCAST SERIES

The Shape of Things to Come

Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future.

Listen now

Opens in a new tab

Flint-interactive

Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications.

Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush.

How to use

1. Use Flint in your chat

Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation.

Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns.

2. Build an interactive app with Flint

Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas.

Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa.

3. Create bespoke interactions

To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks.

Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes.

How it works

Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level:

Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates.

Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states.

Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective.

This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards.

Try it now!

Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery.

App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app.

Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on…

quick_hits.line: Sebastian Raschka released an 11-hour hands-on video course covering reasoning model evaluations, inference scaling, and RL distillation in PyTorch.

item.title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
item.summary: Over 11 hours of coding videos on evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, with Python and PyTorch.
item.content:
I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode.

For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work.

Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content).

We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite).

I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along!

How LLMs, reasoning models, and agents relate and fit together

As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos.

A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well.

A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools.

Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article.

In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.)

So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents.

The resources accompanying these topics shown above are:

The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos

The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below)

The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack

The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system.

Scope and prerequisites

The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation.

Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required.

Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations .

Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered.

The companion book

These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here.

For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises.

The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color!

Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book.

Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials.

The videos

As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription).

The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below.

To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos.

1. Motivation and code setup

The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues.

On the benefits of learning through code implementations

Watch video 1 · Setup instructions

2. Loading a base model, text generation, and KV caching

Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model.

Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient.

These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos.

item.title: v0.40.11
item.summary:
Speech

Ollama can now generate speech on macOS. ollama run plays text or a chat model's reply aloud as the audio is generated, and apps can stream audio through the OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech endpoint.

ollama run phonon " Hello from Ollama. "

d3 decision models

d3 brings vLLM Semantic Router's decision models to Ollama. Give a model text, structured state, or an image, and ask it to classify, answer yes or no, or score options with probabilities. The family includes 2B, 4B, 9B, and 27B sizes.

ollama run d3 " A customer says their card was charged twice. " --ask " Is this a billing issue? "
